passage:
Dear Gopika,
Everyone I know has turned their hobby into something with numbers. Nikhil sells his sourdough, Meenal posts her running times every morning, and even my sketching group asks how many people liked our pages. Last week I realised I hadn't done anything badly, just for fun, in years.
So on Sunday I bought cheap clay and made a lopsided cup that leaks. I laughed so much the neighbours knocked. I am not selling it, not photographing it, not improving it.
Come over next Sunday and make an even worse one? 🙂
Joseph

qa.q: What did Joseph make on Sunday?
qa.a: A lopsided cup that leaks.

qa.q: What does Joseph feel about how friends treat their hobbies, and about the clay cup?
qa.a: Joseph feels a little uneasy noticing that every hobby now comes with numbers, and then delighted at doing something badly just for fun.

qa.q: What invitation does Joseph make, and why might it help Gopika?
qa.a: Joseph invites Gopika to make an even worse cup next Sunday. Doing it badly with no goal gives permission to play without counting anything.

qa.q: How might Gopika feel reading Joseph's letter?
qa.a: Probably amused and glad to be invited, since the letter is warm and jokey. 🙂

grounding: A young adult observes friends turning hobbies into metrics and reclaims doing something badly for fun.

passage:
Last month at a housewarming someone asked me, "Jeevan, what's your record for cycling?" And I had nothing to say. Deepa's baking is a micro-business, Ankit's guitar is a channel, and I felt oddly behind, as if a hobby without a number didn't count.
So I bought a ukulele with a cracked case and now I play it badly, in the bathroom, where nobody hears it and nobody counts it. The other day I realised I'd been smiling for a full hour.
Honestly, being bad at something on purpose feels like a small rebellion, and it keeps me sane.

qa.q: What instrument did Jeevan buy?
qa.a: A ukulele with a cracked case.

qa.q: What did Jeevan feel when friends described their hobbies in numbers?
qa.a: Jeevan felt oddly behind, as if a hobby without a number did not count.

qa.q: What small choice helped Jeevan enjoy play again?
qa.a: Jeevan bought a cheap ukulele and plays it badly in the bathroom, where nobody hears or counts it.

qa.q: How might the friends at the housewarming see their own hobbies?
qa.a: They probably see them as achievements worth measuring or selling, since they speak of a micro-business and a channel.

grounding: A young adult notices friends measuring every hobby and finds relief in doing something badly for fun.

passage:
I'm Amandeep, and I've watched this happen to my whole friend group. Nikita used to bake on Sundays just because the kitchen smelled nice. Now she has a baking page, a posting schedule and a spreadsheet of likes. Last month her cake sank and she almost cried, not because it tasted bad, but because "it won't photograph."
Sameer's running is all pace charts. Farah learned guitar for three weeks, then started pricing online lessons she could teach.
At Nikita's place on Saturday, I pulled out an old box of watercolours and said, "Let's paint something terrible." She hesitated, then painted a purple cow with five legs. She laughed so hard she snorted. I can't say what was going on inside her. But she didn't reach for her phone to take a photo, and at the door she said, "Can we do terrible painting again?"

qa.q: What did Nikita paint on Saturday?
qa.a: A purple cow with five legs.

qa.q: What might Amandeep have felt watching friends turn hobbies into metrics?
qa.a: Amandeep seems sad and a little worried, noticing that Nikita was upset about a sunken cake only because it wouldn't photograph.

qa.q: Why was "Let's paint something terrible" a good invitation?
qa.a: It removed any goal or audience, so Nikita could play badly just for fun.

qa.q: What was the terrible painting like for Nikita?
qa.a: Nikita seemed freed and delighted, laughing till she snorted, leaving her phone alone and asking to do it again.

grounding: Shows an observer noticing friends turning every hobby into a metric and inviting one of them to do something badly for fun.

passage:
March. Hrithik watched Asif play online chess on the metro ride home, jaw tight, checking his rating after every game. "Down eleven points," Asif muttered. "Terrible day." Hrithik remembered when they used to play on a plastic board in college just to talk.
April. At Asif's flat Hrithik pulled out that same plastic board. "New rule: pawns can move backward. No clocks, no ratings." Asif frowned. "That's not real chess." "Exactly." Twenty minutes in, Asif's queen had been captured by a pawn walking in reverse, and he was laughing into a cushion.
May. Asif messaged: "Silly chess Saturday? I invented a rule where knights can swap places." Hrithik noticed he hadn't mentioned his rating in weeks.

qa.q: What new rule did Hrithik bring in April?
qa.a: Pawns can move backward, with no clocks and no ratings.

qa.q: How did Hrithik feel watching Asif on the metro in March?
qa.a: Hrithik felt a little sad and nostalgic, remembering when they played on a plastic board just to talk.

qa.q: What did Hrithik's silly chess rule do for Asif?
qa.a: It took away the score, so Asif could play badly and laugh, and chess became fun again.

qa.q: How had chess changed for Asif by May?
qa.a: Asif was enjoying it again, inventing new rules and no longer talking about his rating.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing a friend turning a hobby into a metric and helping him reclaim it as pure fun.

passage:
Nitin, you ask why I still play the harmonium so badly after thirty years? Let me tell you. When I, Vishal, was twenty-five, my friends and I had a Sunday singing group on the terrace. We sang off-key and ate peanuts. Then Das started recording us to upload. Menon wanted us to enter competitions. Soon we rehearsed with a stopwatch, and people stopped coming.
One evening I watched Das frowning at the number of views, not singing at all. That frightened me more than any deadline at the office.
So I kept a second, secret Sunday. Just me, the old harmonium and whatever came out. No audience, no recording. Some weeks it was awful. It was also the only hour my shoulders came down.
Two years later, Das burnt out and left the office for six months. My silly Sunday hour, I think, is why I didn't.

qa.q: What did Das start doing with the group's singing?
qa.a: Recording them to upload.

qa.q: What did Vishal feel watching Das frown at the view count?
qa.a: Vishal felt frightened, more than by any office deadline, seeing Das not singing at all.

qa.q: Which choice in the story protected Vishal?
qa.a: Keeping a second, secret Sunday hour with the old harmonium, with no audience and no recording, even when it sounded awful.

qa.q: How did the change in the group affect Das?
qa.a: Das got caught up in the views and, two years later, burnt out and left the office for six months.

grounding: Shows a young adult noticing friends turn a shared pastime into metrics and protecting an hour of playing purely for fun.

passage:
It was raining hard in Bengaluru, and Bhavna's plan for a lazy Sunday with friends had shrunk to two hours before everyone's next thing. She noticed it as they sat at Varun's flat.
Varun was showing them his pottery. "I'm going to start selling on a craft site. If I post daily, I can hit a thousand followers by March."
Rukmini said her running was about beating her pace. Arvind had turned his guitar into a video channel with a schedule.
Bhavna felt tired just listening. When had any of them done something just because it was fun, and badly?
She took a sheet of paper and a crayon from Varun's niece's box. "Rule: we draw the rain. Terribly. No photos. No posting."
Varun laughed. "Why?"
"Because nobody's counting."
For forty minutes they drew wobbly clouds and argued about purple rain. Varun's was the worst. He was grinning the whole time.

qa.q: How many followers did Varun hope to reach by March?
qa.a: Varun hoped to hit a thousand followers by March.

qa.q: What was Bhavna feeling as her friends described their hobbies?
qa.a: Bhavna felt tired and a little sad, noticing that none of them did anything just for fun anymore.

qa.q: What small step did Bhavna take, and why might it help?
qa.a: She set up a no-posting, draw-it-badly game, which let everyone play purely for fun and rest from constant goals.

qa.q: How did Varun experience drawing the rain?
qa.a: Varun enjoyed it and relaxed, grinning the whole time even though his drawing was the worst.

grounding: A young adult notices friends turn every hobby into a metric and starts a purely-for-fun game, reclaiming play.
